newsitem.title: KENYA: INTERVIEW - Nairobi bourse chief wants further ref.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Nairobi bourse chief wants further ref.

text.p: Nairobi Stock Exchange chairman Jimnah Mbaru on Wednesday urged the government to rein-in runaway interest rates, improve infrastructure and ease restrictions on foreign investors to help the Kenyan bourse attain real growth.

Mbaru told Reuters in an interview rules that barred foreign portfolio investors from buying shares of foreign-controlled companies effectively locked them out of 70 percent of the 59 listed companies and more importantly, the blue chips.

Under Kenyan laws, foreign portfolio investors may purchase shares only in locally-controlled companies. These make up just 30 percent of the listed companies and would not necessarily be of core interest to these portfolio investors, Mbaru said.
"We need foreign portfolio investors to be allowed to buy 40 percent of foreign-controlled companies," Mbaru said.
Mbaru said that a growth in manufacturing and a faster pace of privatising government companies would also lift the bourse.
Manufacturing contributes just 13 percent of Kenya's gross domestic product (GDP) and Mbaru saw a growth of about 20-25 percent as suficient to get the Nairobi bourse "very vibrant".
Mbaru also foresaw the trading of government treasury bills and government bonds on the bourse as well as fully privatising the power sector.

Mbaru said that public education about share trading was still very poor in Kenya and investors often bought shares and held onto them for a long time. "If there is more education, people will be aware of the need to trade in their shares."
"The government should continue on a path to create what we call an enabling environment," Mbaru told Reuters.

"Infrastructure here is in a pathetic situation. There are power shortages, vehicles are destroyed by too many potholes, telephone lines sometimes do not work and sometimes there isn't a steady supply of clean water. We need action there," he said.

Mbaru said a reduction in interest rates would turn foreign investment attention to the equities market. He said government interest rates of up to 22 percent on treasury bills meant that investors were preoccupied by a lucrative money market.
He said investors were wary that with upcoming elections, money supply would rocket to levels last seen in 1992. That would erode their investment and put inflation beyond control.

In 1992, money printed to finance landmark pluralist elections led to inflation reaching 101 percent. It has since been reduced to a single digit level and Central Bank Governor Micah Cheserem has pledged the 1992 mistakes would be avoided.
At December 1995, the Nairobi Stock Exchange was capitalised at $1.89 billion. The Johannesburg Stock Exchange is by far Africa's largest.
